stops.name: Gateway Arch
stops.teaser: A stainless-steel arch that took more than two years to build, and nobody has been able to out-tall it.
stops.map: Gateway Arch National Park, 11 N 4th St, St. Louis, MO
stops.clue: Go to the Mississippi riverfront downtown. Look for a huge shiny arch with its legs on the grass, high above the park.
stops.safety: The park has a lot of steps and open lawns. Stay on paths, mind the traffic near the park roads, and check the tram and tower schedule if you plan to go up.

story: Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen designed the Arch in 1947. The idea came from civic leader Luther Ely Smith, who proposed a memorial on the riverfront in 1933. Construction began on February 12, 1963, and was finished on October 28, 1965.
The Arch is 630 feet tall, clad in stainless steel and shaped as a weighted catenary arch. It is the world's tallest arch. It cost $13 million and opened to the public on June 10, 1967.
It stands at the 1764 site of the founding of St. Louis, and honors the westward expansion of the United States. It is nicknamed the Gateway to the West.
stops.fact: The finished Arch opened to visitors in 1967.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Arch opened when its last piece went in. Wikipedia says it was completed on October 28, 1965, and opened to the public on June 10, 1967.

claims.t: The Gateway Arch is the world's tallest arch.
claims.why: Wikipedia: it is the world's tallest arch.
Saarinen designed it in 1947. Construction began in 1963.

spot.q: The photo shows the Arch nearly finished in September 1965. How tall is it?
spot.why: The Arch is 630 feet tall, clad in stainless steel. It is the world's tallest arch.

stops.name: Eads Bridge
stops.teaser: The oldest bridge on the Mississippi, and the first to lean on steel.
stops.clue: Go to the riverfront just north of the Arch. Look for a long bridge with three big arches over the water and a stone pier on the shore.
stops.safety: The roadway and rail lines share the bridge. Use the sidewalk, watch for trains and bikes, and stay behind the rail.

story: The bridge is named for James Buchanan Eads, who designed and built it. Work began in 1867 and ended in 1874. Eads had no experience building bridges. It was the first bridge across the Mississippi south of the Missouri River, and it is the oldest bridge on the river.

The foundations went more than 100 feet below the water, deeper than anything built underwater before. They used pneumatic caissons, the largest ever built at the time. The center arch is 520 feet long, the longest rigid span in the world then.
The highway deck was closed to cars from 1991 to 2003 and now carries cars and people again. The old railroad deck carries the MetroLink light rail.
stops.fact: Its foundations are more than 100 feet below the river.
stops.disputed: Many people credit the Brooklyn Bridge with pioneering these methods. Wikipedia says the Eads Bridge pioneered them, and its work began in 1867, three years before the Brooklyn Bridge.

stops.name: St. Louis Union Station
stops.teaser: A train station that was once the busiest in the world, and now is a hotel.
stops.map: St. Louis Union Station, 1820 Market St, St. Louis, MO
stops.clue: Go to Market Street west of downtown. Look for a huge stone building with a tall clock tower and a big arched entrance.
stops.safety: Market Street has traffic and light rail. Use crosswalks, and remember that it is now a hotel and entertainment center, so check the hours for what you want to see.

story: The station opened on September 1, 1894. Theodore Link designed it, and George Pegram designed its 11.5-acre train shed. It was the world's largest and busiest railroad station when it opened, and its shed had the largest roof span in the world.

The Grand Hall has gold leaf, Romanesque arches and a barrel-vaulted ceiling 65 feet high. It was enlarged in 1903 for the 1904 World's Fair. At its peak in the 1940s, it handled 100,000 passengers a day.
The last Amtrak passenger train left in 1978. In the 1980s the building was renovated as a hotel, shopping center and entertainment complex.
stops.disputed: Many people do not know where the famous photo of Truman holding the wrong "Dewey Defeats Truman" headline was taken. Wikipedia says it was shot at this station in 1948.

stops.name: Wainwright Building
stops.teaser: One of the first skyscrapers that looked like a skyscraper.
stops.map: Wainwright Building, 709 Chestnut St, St. Louis, MO
stops.clue: Go to Chestnut Street downtown, near the Arch. Look for a dark red building, 10 stories tall, with tall vertical lines and decorated edges.
stops.safety: Chestnut Street has traffic and parking garages nearby. Use crosswalks, and note it is a state office building with security at the door.

story: Brewer Ellis Wainwright commissioned the building because he needed offices for the St. Louis Brewers Association. Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan designed it, and it was built from 1890 to 1891. It is 10 stories and 135 feet tall.

Architect Frank Lloyd Wright called it "the very first human expression of a tall steel office-building as Architecture." In 2013 it was named one of the "10 Buildings That Changed America" in a PBS series. Sullivan is sometimes called the Father of Skyscrapers.
The building became a National Historic Landmark in 1968. The National Trust for Historic Preservation rescued it from demolition, and Missouri later bought it as part of a state office complex.
stops.disputed: Many people assume the building was always a state office building. Wikipedia says it was built for Ellis Wainwright, a brewer, to house the St. Louis Brewers Association.

spot.why: Frank Lloyd Wright praised it that way. Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan designed it, and it was built from 1890 to 1891.
